pages.text: The counter reads 3 unknowns and 3 equations. Rows 1 and 3 hold `+z` and `−z`, so adding them cancels z. `2x + 3y = 8` drops into a new stack.

pages.alt: A counter reads unknowns 3, x, y, z, and equations 3. Three rows: x + y + z = 6; 2x minus  y + z = 3; x + 2y minus  z = 2. New stack: 2x + 3y + 0 = 8, one row so far.

pages.name: Remove it again
pages.task: Now remove z from rows 2 and 3. Which row drops into the new stack?
pages.why: Row 2 has `+z` and row 3 has `−z`, opposite signs, so add them. `2x + x = 3x`, `−y + 2y = y`, `z − z = 0` and `3 + 2 = 5`. Now both new rows hold only x and y, so the counter reads 2 and 2. In one study, on one problem, 76% of students misjudged the operations to use when eliminating.

pages.name: Two and two
pages.text: Both new rows hold only x and y, so they slide into the picture from Elimination. Three times the top row, `9x + 3y = 15`, take away the bottom row, leaves `7x = 7`, so x = 1. Two removals of the same letter took three rows to two, and this one takes two to one: each step down loses one unknown and one equation, which is [[stepping down]].

pages.name: Put them back
pages.task: x = 1. Put it back into `3x + y = 5` for y, then x and y into row 1 for z. Which is (x, y, z)?
pages.why: `3 + y = 5`, so y = 5 − 3 = 2. Then row 1 gives `1 + 2 + z = 6`, so z = 6 − 1 − 2 = 3. All three rows fit (1, 2, 3).

Answers put in: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 true; 2 minus  2 + 3 = 3 true; 1 + 4 minus  3 = 2 true. The two new rows: 9x + 3y = 15; 2x + 3y = 8. Sum row: 7x + 0 = 7. pages.name: Check all three
pages.text: Put (1, 2, 3) into all three rows, because a slip can fit one row and fail another. Row 3 gives `1 + 2 × 2 − 3 = 2`, and rows 1 and 2 fit as well.

pages.alt: A counter reads unknowns 1, x, and equations 1. Rows 1 to 3, small: x + y + z = 6; 2x minus  y + z = 3; x + 2y minus  z = 2. Answers put in: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 true; 2 minus  2 + 3 = 3 true; 1 + 4 minus  3 = 2 true. The two new rows: 9x + 3y = 15; 2x + 3y = 8. Sum row: 7x + 0 = 7. A graph 0 to 4 across and 0 to 7 up draws the top row solid and the bottom row dashed, and the sum row dotted, upright at x = 1, with the crossing ringed.

pages.name: The same letter
pages.task: Back to the start, with `2x + 3y = 8` from rows 1 and 3. Which second removal lets the new stack slide on?
pages.why: Take the same letter from a different pair. Rows 2 and 3 added give `3x + y = 5`, so both new rows hold x and y, 2 unknowns in 2 equations. Taking y from rows 1 and 2 instead gives `3x + 2z = 9`, and the two new rows would still hold x, y and z.

pages.name: The circuit
pages.text: All three currents are kept as unknowns. The junction law gives row 1, and the loop law round each loop gives rows 2 and 3, as the working shows. Row 1 at × 2 holds `−2I₃`, so adding row 3 removes I₃.

pages.task: Solve `x + y + z = 9`, `x + 2y − z = 4` and `3x − y + 2z = 11`. Which is (x, y, z)?
pages.why: Rows 1 and 2 added give `2x + 3y = 13`, and row 2 at × 2 added to row 3 gives `5x + 3y = 19`. Take away, and `3x = 6`, so x = 2. Then `4 + 3y = 13`, so y = 3, and row 1 gives z = 9 − 2 − 3 = 4.

pages.task: Solve `2x + y + z = 7`, `x − y + 2z = 5` and `3x + y − z = 2`. Which is (x, y, z)?
pages.why: y is `−y` in row 2 and `+y` in rows 1 and 3, so add row 2 to each. That gives `3x + 3z = 12` and `4x + z = 7`. Three times the second, take away the first, and `9x = 9`, so x = 1. Then z = 7 − 4 = 3, and row 1 gives y = 7 − 2 − 3 = 2.

pages.alt: A counter reads unknowns 1, x, and equations 1. Rows 1 to 3, small: 2x + y + z = 7; x minus  y + 2z = 5; 3x + y minus  z = 2. Answers put in: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 true; 1 minus  2 + 6 = 5 true; 3 + 2 minus  3 = 2 true. The two new rows: 12x + 3z = 21; 3x + 3z = 12. Sum row: 9x + 0 = 9. A graph 0 to 4 across and 0 to 7 up draws the top row solid and the bottom row dashed, and the sum row dotted, upright at x = 1, with the crossing ringed.

pages.task: Last one, with the new batteries. Which currents I₁, I₂ and I₃ fit all three rows?
pages.why: Row 1 plus row 3 gives `I₁ + 2I₂ = 10`, and row 1 plus row 2 gives `2I₁ + I₂ = 14`. Twice that, take away the first, and `3I₁ = 18`, so I₁ = 6 A. Then I₂ = 14 − 12 = 2 A, and row 2 gives I₃ = 14 − 6 = 8 A. To solve large systems, you set the numbers in front of the letters out as a block called a matrix: that is the Matrices course.
